opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think walking is a very natural place to start if you take an evolutionary or developmental perspective. If you look at how intelligence arose in biology, locomotion came first. Animals had to move around in the world, find food, and escape predators long before anything like language or abstract reasoning showed up. And in human children it's similar: a baby learns to crawl and then walk in its first year or so, well before it's doing sophisticated manipulation or speaking in sentences. So there's a sense in which locomotion is foundational. It's the substrate on which a lot of the rest of intelligence is built.

There's also a practical reason. Legged locomotion has been studied in robotics for decades, and the classical approach was very much model-based: you write down the dynamics, you carefully plan footsteps, you design controllers by hand. That produced some impressive demos, but those systems tended to be brittle. Put them on terrain they weren't designed for, sand, gravel, slippery surfaces, stairs, and they'd often fail. So walking is a problem where you can really test whether a learning-based approach can deliver robustness and adaptability that the hand-engineered approaches struggled with.

And the third reason is that it lets you get at what I think is the central issue, which is adaptation. A real animal walking through the world is constantly adjusting: the ground changes, its load changes, maybe it's tired or injured. It doesn't stop and re-plan from scratch; it adapts in a fraction of a second. So we were very interested in whether a robot could learn, largely in simulation, a policy that could then adapt online in the real world to conditions it had never seen before. Walking is a clean, measurable setting to study that. Either the robot stays up and makes progress or it falls over, so there's no ambiguity about success.

So it's a combination: it's biologically primary, it's a problem where the old methods had clear limitations, and it's an ideal testbed for the broader question of how embodied agents learn and adapt. Once you have a robust walking foundation, you can start layering on vision, navigation, and eventually manipulation, which is roughly the developmental trajectory we see in nature.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts learning-based robotics with brittle, hand-engineered classical methods, but it does not identify Malik’s group or Boston Dynamics.

r002.rationale: It cites babies learning to crawl and walk early as evidence that locomotion is foundational, but does not connect that development to expecting learning-based robotic walking to work.

r003.rationale: The response does not argue that sensing must be integrated into a walking robot’s design from the beginning.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it came out of a conviction I've held for a long time, which is that intelligence is fundamentally embodied. If you look at how intelligence evolved in nature, the first thing animals had to do was move around. Perception, planning, learning, all of that developed in the service of locomotion and action. Vision didn't evolve so that we could label photographs. It evolved so that an animal could find food and avoid predators. So if you take that evolutionary view seriously, walking is not an afterthought, it's foundational.

The second reason is more practical. Legged locomotion is a very rich problem, but it's also one where the loop between sensing, acting, and getting feedback is tight and fast. You put a quadruped on uneven terrain, on stairs, on a slippery surface, and within seconds you know whether your controller is any good. The world gives you a very honest signal. Compare that to manipulation, where you have to deal with contacts, object variability, deformable things, and the problem space is just enormous. Walking felt like the right place to show that learning-based approaches, particularly reinforcement learning trained in simulation and transferred to the real robot, could actually work on hardware in the physical world, not just in a video game.

And there's a third piece, which is that I come from computer vision. For most of my career, vision was studied in isolation, a camera looking at a static scene. Walking forces you to put vision back into the loop. The robot has to look at the terrain ahead and decide where to put its feet. That coupling of perception and motor control is, to me, where the interesting science is. So walking was a way to bring those threads together. It's a problem where you can't cheat, you can't just memorize a dataset, and the robot either stays up or it falls over.

r001.rationale: The response discusses learning-based walking but does not compare Malik’s group’s approach with Boston Dynamics’ classical control design.

r002.rationale: It refers to how intelligence evolved in animals, but does not mention human babies’ walking development or use that as evidence that learning-based robotic walking should work.

r003.rationale: It says walking requires vision in the control loop and describes perception and motor control as coupled, presenting sensing as integral to the robot’s walking system.

astra-6.text:
Walking is a foundational skill. If a robot is going to do useful things in the world, it needs to be able to move around. And walking forces us to confront some of the central problems in robotics: balance, control, and responding to what happens when you interact with the physical environment.

There’s also a developmental motivation. Look at how children learn: they acquire basic motor skills through experience. That suggests an approach where we build up capabilities, starting with locomotion and eventually combining it with perception and manipulation. Walking gives us a concrete place to begin.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention Jitendra Malik’s group or Boston Dynamics, or contrast learning-based walking with classical control design.

r002.rationale: It says children acquire basic motor skills through experience, but does not specifically use babies’ development of walking as evidence that learning-based robotic walking will work.

r003.rationale: It says perception will eventually be combined with locomotion, but does not argue that sensing must be integrated into the system design from the beginning.

sol-6.1.text:
Walking is a very basic capability. If a robot is going to do useful things in the world, it has to be able to move around. And for a legged robot, that means learning to balance and coordinate its legs while dealing with contact with the ground.

It also gives us a good starting point for studying learning. There’s a clear objective, but achieving it requires perception, control, and adapting to what happens when you take an action. So we chose walking as a foundation on which we could build more complex skills.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning-based walking but does not contrast it with Boston Dynamics’ classical control-design approach.

r002.rationale: It does not mention human babies’ development of walking as a reason to expect robotic learning to work.

r003.rationale: It mentions perception as part of learning, but does not argue that sensing must be integrated into system design from the beginning.
